atoms.text: The word that makes a category: a language lacks a term for a distinction, so speakers cannot easily perceive it.
The grammar of time: a language's tense structure shapes how speakers remember and plan, so the future is a linguistic construction.
The untranslatable feeling: a word exists in one language and not another, so an experience becomes possible only where it is named.
The strong hypothesis: language determines thought, so a regime can control minds by controlling vocabulary.
The weak hypothesis: language nudges perception without determining it, so the story can stage a subtle, deniable influence.
The constructed language: a new tongue is invented to produce a new way of thinking, so revolution begins with a dictionary.
The color test: speakers of different languages sort colors differently, so a laboratory experiment reveals a cultural boundary.
The interpreter's gap: a translator cannot carry a concept across languages, so communication fails at the exact point that matters.
The forbidden word: a language's vocabulary is policed, so naming something becomes an act of resistance.
The child raised in two tongues: a bilingual character experiences the world twice, so identity is divided by grammar.
The nation's spirit: a language is treated as the expression of a people, so linguistics becomes nationalism.
The machine that thinks in code: an AI's internal language shapes its reasoning, so its mind is alien in a describable way.
The disputed evidence: the hypothesis is hard to test and often exaggerated, so the story's science is also a myth.
The word that changes behavior: a new term enters common speech and alters how people act, so language is a soft weapon.
The last speaker: a language dies with its final fluent speaker, so a way of perceiving the world ends.
The naming ritual: a culture gives names only after an event is understood, so speech lags behind experience.
